evidence.claim: Century Drive climbs steadily from Bend into the Deschutes National Forest, then the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway runs past Mount Bachelor and south along the Cascades.
evidence.quote: From the outskirts of town, Century Drive (Oregon Route 372) climbs steadily into the Deschutes National Forest.

evidence.claim: then the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway runs past Mount Bachelor and south along the Cascades.
evidence.quote: west into the Deschutes National Forest and past the Mt. Bachelor Ski Area, then south along the Cascades

evidence.claim: Oregon DOT gives the drive 66 miles and three to five hours.
evidence.quote: Distance: 66 miles Minimum Driving Time: 3-5 hours

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration describes this National Scenic Byway through its lava flows, alpine lakes and meadows.
evidence.quote: National Scenic Byway • Oregon

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration describes this National Scenic Byway through its lava flows, alpine lakes and meadows.
evidence.quote: See outstanding examples of lava flows, alpine lakes, and meadows.

evidence.claim: The geological variety is visible from the road: west of Bend, a lava flow that changed the Deschutes River’s course comes into view.
evidence.quote: A few miles further west, a vast lava flow that altered the river's course can be seen from the road.

evidence.claim: Oregon DOT traces Century Drive’s name to a 100-mile dirt road of horse-and-buggy days.
evidence.quote: In the days of the horse and buggy, it was a 100-mile dirt road—hence the name!

evidence.claim: A primitive road from Bend reached Elk Lake in 1920, helping make the lake a summer recreation destination.
evidence.quote: A primitive road was built from Bend to Elk Lake in 1920.  The road helped make Elk Lake a popular recreation site

evidence.claim: Growing visitor numbers brought more ranger work, and the Forest Service built Elk Lake Guard Station in 1929 to support that presence.
evidence.quote: Since the land around Elk Lake was administered by the Forest Service, the growing number of visitors required the rangers in Bend to spend more time in the area.  To support this presence, the Elk Lake Guard Station was built in 1929.

evidence.claim: From Bend, travel west past Mount Bachelor to Todd Lake, then Sparks Lake and Devils Lake.
evidence.quote: Soon, you'll reach Todd Lake, the first of a dozen Cascade gems

evidence.claim: From Bend, travel west past Mount Bachelor to Todd Lake, then Sparks Lake and Devils Lake.
evidence.quote: Beyond Mount Bachelor Ski Area, the byway passes Todd Lake, Sparks Lake, Devils Lake, Elk Lake, Hosmer Lake, Lava Lake, Little Lava Lake, and Cultus Lake.

evidence.claim: Continue south past Elk Lake toward Lava Lake and Little Lava Lake, where the Deschutes begins.
evidence.quote: Nearby Little Lava Lake is the source of the Deschutes River

evidence.claim: Continue south past Elk Lake toward Lava Lake and Little Lava Lake, where the Deschutes begins.
evidence.quote: A few miles south, you'll reach Elk Lake

evidence.claim: The young river runs through a meadow beside the byway on the way toward Cultus Lake and Crane Prairie Reservoir.
evidence.quote: which meanders through a lush meadow along the Byway as you move south toward Cultus Lake and Crane Prairie Reservoir.

evidence.claim: Beyond Crane Prairie, the road continues south to Davis Lake and ends at Oregon Route 58 near Crescent and Odell lakes.
evidence.quote: The Byway ends at Oregon Route 58 near Crescent and Odell lakes

evidence.claim: Beyond Crane Prairie, the road continues south to Davis Lake
evidence.quote: The Byway continues south to Davis Lake

evidence.claim: West of Bend, a lava flow that altered the Deschutes River’s course is visible from the road.
evidence.quote: A few miles further west, a vast lava flow that altered the river's course can be seen from the road.

evidence.claim: The road closes beyond Mount Bachelor in winter. Oregon DOT lists June–October as the best visiting season.
evidence.quote: Best Time to Visit: June-October (the road closes beyond Mt. Bachelor in the winter).

evidence.claim: Sparks Lake loses water through openings along its southwest shore rather than a visible outlet stream.
evidence.quote: While Sparks Lake has no visible outflow into the Deschutes River basin, the lake can be observed flowing into crevasses and outcrops along the South West shores.

evidence.claim: Lava flows from the Three Sisters and Mount Bachelor systems formed its closed basin.
evidence.quote: Sparks lake lies in a closed basin formed by lava flows of the Three Sisters and Mt. Bachelor volcanic systems

evidence.claim: Snowmelt from South Sister and Broken Top feeds it.
evidence.quote: Sparks Lake is fed by snow melt from South Sister and Broken Top mountains.

evidence.claim: Sediment and vegetation have partly filled what was once a larger lake.
evidence.quote: the water body is a remnant of a bigger lake that has partly filled with sediment and vegetation.

evidence.claim: Mount Bachelor, the Three Sisters and Broken Top are visible from the lake, putting the water beside the volcanic peaks that frame it.
evidence.quote: Many of the region's mountain peaks, such as Mount Bachelor, Three Sisters, and Broken Top, are visible from the lake.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service maintains a boat launch here, with a parking area and a trail beside the lake.
evidence.quote: The United States Forest Service maintains a boat launch at Sparks Lake. The site has a parking area, a lake trail

evidence.claim: Water flows into crevices and outcrops along the southwest shore.
evidence.quote: the lake can be observed flowing into crevasses and outcrops along the South West shores.

evidence.claim: At Devils Lake, clear water and a shallow white pumice bottom create an optical illusion: boats can seem suspended above the lakebed.
evidence.quote: crystal clear water and a shallow white pumice bottom make it seem as if boats on the surface are floating in midair.

evidence.claim: The lake covers 23 acres at an elevation of 5,446 feet.
evidence.quote: Devils Lake is a shallow, 23 acre lake located in Deschutes County, Oregon, along the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway and found at an elevation of 5,446 feet

evidence.claim: The surrounding volcanic country also became a training ground for astronauts preparing for the Apollo missions in the mid-1960s.
evidence.quote: In the mid-1960s, astronauts trained along the Cascade Lakes Highway in preparation for the Apollo missions to the moon.

evidence.claim: Oregon DOT records that Jim Irwin left a rock from a volcanic dome near Devils Lake on the lunar surface during Apollo 15 in 1971.
evidence.quote: In 1971, Astronaut Jim Irwin of the Apollo 15 mission placed an earth rock from a volcanic dome near Devils Lake on the lunar surface.

evidence.claim: Clear water lies over a shallow white pumice bottom.
evidence.quote: crystal clear water and a shallow white pumice bottom

evidence.claim: Solidified lava separates Lava Lake from Little Lava Lake and is visible along both shorelines.
evidence.quote: It is a close neighbor of Little Lava Lake, from which it is separated by solidified lava.

evidence.claim: Solidified lava separates Lava Lake from Little Lava Lake and is visible along both shorelines.
evidence.quote: Solidified lava flows are visible along the shorelines of both lakes

evidence.claim: Flows from Mount Bachelor changed the local drainage patterns, forming these neighboring lakes.
evidence.quote: Lava Lake, Little Lava Lake, and other nearby lakes are volcanogenic, having formed after lava flows from Mount Bachelor altered drainage patterns in the area.

evidence.claim: The two lakes sit in the Deschutes National Forest; Lava Lake’s elevation is 4,740 feet, and Little Lava Lake’s is 4,744 feet.
evidence.quote: Lava Lake is at an elevation of 4,740 feet (1,440 m) in the Deschutes National Forest.

evidence.claim: Little Lava Lake’s is 4,744 feet.
evidence.quote: Little Lava Lake is at an elevation of 4,744 feet (1,446 m) in the Deschutes National Forest.

evidence.claim: Lava Lake covers 368 acres and averages 20 feet deep.
evidence.quote: The lake covers 368 acres (149 ha) to an average depth of 20 feet

evidence.claim: To the north, Broken Top and South Sister rise into view.
evidence.quote: the volcanic peaks Broken Top and South Sister can be seen to the north.

evidence.claim: At nearby Little Lava Lake, the Deschutes starts as a small creek flowing south before its later turn north toward the Columbia.
evidence.quote: The Deschutes River begins as a small creek trickling south out of Little Lava Lake

evidence.claim: before its later turn north toward the Columbia.
evidence.quote: before turning north toward its long trek to the Columbia.

evidence.claim: Solidified lava is visible along the shores of Lava Lake and Little Lava Lake.
evidence.quote: Solidified lava flows are visible along the shorelines of both lakes

flags: Century Drive name origins conflict: Oregon DOT says a 100-mile dirt road; Wikipedia says centennial paving. The overview attributes the DOT account and does not combine them.
The material strip runs opposite the Bend-to-Route-58 narrative. Moments follow the explicit DOT driving sequence, preserving their exact titles, coordinates and existing motifs.
The dated practical note checks the saved DOT page’s general winter closure, not live road status. Archived FHWA mentions permits without usable current details; no permit regime is invented.

Devils Lake’s Apollo-rock account is attributed to Oregon DOT; no NASA corroboration is cached. Its unsupported-by-scientific-evidence unique-earth-rock superlative is omitted. Published length is 66 miles, not the catalog’s 68.6 mapped miles.
Devils Lake is kept shorter than 90 words because the site-specific cache is brief; no extra observations or visitor logistics have been added to stretch it.
